title: Nash Basics
question: A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which no player can improve by changing only their own move.
correctExplanation: True. Each player's choice is the best response to the others', so no one gains from a solo change.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The definition concerns unilateral deviation — everyone is doing the best they can given what the others are doing.
lessonContent:
Stability means no profitable solo change.
Best responses hold each choice in place.
Equilibrium is about mutual consistency.
Check each player one at a time.
Share this: ask whether any party could improve by acting alone.

title: Group Optimum
question: If a set of strategies is a Nash equilibrium, it must also give every player the best outcome the group could achieve.
correctExplanation: False. Stable arrangements can be collectively poor, as the prisoner's dilemma famously shows.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. No player can improve alone, yet all might improve together — that gap is the heart of the dilemma.
lessonContent:
Stable and optimal are different tests.
Joint improvement can be possible at equilibrium.
Efficiency requires cooperation, not just stability.
Ask whether everyone could gain together.
Share this: find one stable arrangement that everyone dislikes.

title: Prisoners Choice
question: The prisoner's dilemma shows that individually rational choices can leave everyone worse off than if they had cooperated.
correctExplanation: True. Each player's safest individual move leads to a jointly inferior result.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Rationality at the individual level does not guarantee a good outcome for the pair, which is the paradox.
lessonContent:
Individual and collective incentives can conflict.
Good personal choices may produce poor shared outcomes.
Structure, not character, drives the result.
Look for ways to change the incentives.
Share this: name one situation where acting safely hurts everyone.

title: Mutual Cooperation
question: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is the Nash equilibrium.
correctExplanation: False. Mutual defection is the equilibrium; each player is tempted to defect whatever the other does.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Cooperation would be better for both, but each has an incentive to break it alone, so it cannot hold.
lessonContent:
Equilibrium follows incentives, not desirability.
Temptation breaks otherwise good arrangements.
The best joint outcome may be unstable.
Check each player's temptation to defect.
Share this: note one agreement vulnerable to a solo defection.

title: Dominant Move
question: A dominant strategy is one that is best for a player no matter what the other players choose.
correctExplanation: True. It outperforms the alternatives across every possible response from others.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Dominance is a strong property: the choice does not depend on predicting what others will do.
lessonContent:
Dominance means never needing to predict.
A robust choice wins across scenarios.
Few real decisions have this property.
Look for options that are safe everywhere.
Share this: find one option that is reasonable whatever happens.

title: How Many Equilibria
question: Every game has exactly one Nash equilibrium.
correctExplanation: False. Games can have none in pure strategies, one, or several.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Some games have multiple equilibria and others none until mixed strategies are allowed.
lessonContent:
Multiplicity is common in games.
Some games have no stable pure choice.
Mixed strategies can supply an equilibrium.
Check all the possibilities rather than assuming one.
Share this: consider whether a situation has more than one stable outcome.

title: Matching Pennies
question: Matching pennies has no Nash equilibrium in pure strategies.
correctExplanation: True. Whatever pair of moves you pick, one player would rather switch, so only a mixed strategy stabilises it.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Each pure pair invites a profitable deviation, so the equilibrium exists only in randomised play.
lessonContent:
Some games reward unpredictability.
Randomising can restore stability.
Pure choices may never settle.
Think in probabilities when no move is safe.
Share this: name one situation where being predictable is a disadvantage.

title: Mixed Strategy
question: A mixed strategy means choosing randomly among your available moves according to set probabilities.
correctExplanation: True. Players randomise over options, often to keep an opponent from predicting them.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The randomness is deliberate and weighted, not careless, and it can be the stable way to play.
lessonContent:
Deliberate randomness can be optimal.
Unpredictability protects against exploitation.
Probabilities can be tuned.
Mix only when pure choices fail.
Share this: notice one contest where surprise has value.

title: Dominant Pair
question: If both players have a dominant strategy, the resulting combination is the unique Nash equilibrium.
correctExplanation: True. When each picks their best-everywhere option, no one can gain by switching alone.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mutual dominance pins the outcome down uniquely, which is why these games are easy to predict.
lessonContent:
Dominance simplifies prediction.
When both sides are locked in, the result is clear.
Strong structure reduces uncertainty.
Check dominance before forecasting.
Share this: identify one situation with a forced choice on both sides.

title: Efficiency Promise
question: A Nash equilibrium always produces an efficient, waste-free outcome.
correctExplanation: False. Equilibria can be stable and still wasteful, as arms races and commons problems show.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Stability says nothing about whether resources are well used; everyone may be stuck in a poor but rational pattern.
lessonContent:
Stability can coexist with waste.
Rational behaviour may preserve inefficiency.
Efficiency needs its own analysis.
Distinguish a settled outcome from a good one.
Share this: find one stable practice that wastes something.

title: Traffic Side
question: Choosing which side of the road to drive on is a coordination game with more than one possible equilibrium.
correctExplanation: True. Driving on the left or the right can both be stable, as long as everyone agrees.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Either convention works once adopted, which is why coordination games often have multiple equilibria.
lessonContent:
Some outcomes need agreement, not correctness.
Either convention can be stable.
The hardest part is choosing together.
Standardisation creates value on its own.
Share this: name one convention whose value lies only in everyone sharing it.

title: Focal Point
question: A focal point is an obvious option that helps players coordinate without communicating.
correctExplanation: True. Shared expectations can settle an ambiguous coordination problem on one choice.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Prominence does the work: people converge on the option that stands out to everyone at once.
lessonContent:
Shared expectation can replace communication.
Prominence guides coordination.
Culture shapes what counts as obvious.
Look for the salient option.
Share this: pick where to meet a friend without discussing it.

title: Repeated Game
question: In a prisoner's dilemma played repeatedly, cooperation can be sustained as an equilibrium.
correctExplanation: True. When the game repeats, future consequences can make cooperation the better long-run choice.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The shadow of the future changes incentives, so reciprocity can hold where a single round would collapse.
lessonContent:
Repetition changes incentives.
Future consequences discipline present temptation.
Trust can build through reciprocity.
The shadow of the future matters.
Share this: notice one relationship sustained by repeated interaction.

title: Stag Hunt
question: The stag hunt shows that a safe, moderate outcome can be a stable equilibrium even when a better one exists.
correctExplanation: True. Fear of being let down can hold players at a lower but safer payoff.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Both the grand prize and the safe fallback can be equilibria, and risk attitudes decide which one settles.
lessonContent:
Risk and reward trade off in games.
Safe fallbacks can trap players.
Trust enables better equilibria.
Ask what would justify the bolder choice.
Share this: weigh one safe option against a better but riskier one.

title: Trust Not Required
question: For a Nash equilibrium to hold, players must trust one another.
correctExplanation: False. Trust is irrelevant to the definition; stability comes from incentives, not goodwill.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Even suspicious players stay put if switching would cost them, which is what equilibrium requires.
lessonContent:
Incentives, not trust, stabilise outcomes.
People can settle while distrusting each other.
Goodwill is a separate question.
Look at payoffs, not intentions.
Share this: find one stable arrangement held by incentives rather than trust.

title: Cheap Talk
question: Cheap talk is communication that costs nothing and so may not be credible.
correctExplanation: True. Words without a cost or commitment can be ignored, since anyone could say them.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Because talk is free, it carries little information unless backed by something at stake.
lessonContent:
Free promises are weak signals.
Costly commitments carry information.
Ask what a speaker risks by talking.
Credibility must be earned or burned.
Share this: distinguish one commitment from mere talk.

title: Commons Overuse
question: In the tragedy of the commons, shared resources are overused even though everyone would gain from restraint.
correctExplanation: True. Each user captures the full benefit of taking more while sharing the cost of depletion.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Private gain and shared loss push each individual toward overuse, leaving the group worse off.
lessonContent:
Shared costs and private gains invite overuse.
Individual logic erodes collective goods.
Rules or prices can realign incentives.
Design matters more than goodwill.
Share this: name one shared resource you use and its cost.

title: Solve Backward
question: Backward induction solves sequential games by reasoning from the final move back to the first.
correctExplanation: True. Starting at the end pins down each earlier choice, because players anticipate what follows.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Working backwards removes options that would not be chosen later, narrowing the path from the start.
lessonContent:
Sequential games are solved from the end.
Later moves constrain earlier ones.
Anticipation shapes present choices.
Reason backward to find the path.
Share this: plan a multi-step decision starting from its last step.

title: Credible Threats
question: Subgame perfect equilibrium rules out threats that a player would not actually carry out.
correctExplanation: True. Only promises and threats that are rational to execute survive the analysis.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. A threat you would not follow through on is discounted, so the equilibrium ignores it.
lessonContent:
Threats must be worth executing.
Talk that would not be carried out is discounted.
Credibility is checked at each decision point.
Test whether you would really follow through.
Share this: examine whether one of your threats is credible.

title: Nested Games
question: Every Nash equilibrium of a sequential game is also subgame perfect.
correctExplanation: False. Some equilibria rely on non-credible threats and fail the stronger subgame perfect test.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Subgame perfection is a stricter requirement, so it excludes equilibria that ordinary stability would allow.
lessonContent:
Some tests are stricter than others.
Stability can rest on empty threats.
Stronger criteria screen them out.
Nested reasoning exposes weaknesses.
Share this: find one plan that survives only through a bluff.

title: Tit for Tat
question: Tit for tat is a repeated-game strategy that starts by cooperating, then copies the opponent's previous move.
correctExplanation: True. It rewards cooperation and punishes defection in equal measure, which keeps it simple and effective.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The strategy is nice first, retaliatory when wronged, and forgiving once the other side cooperates again.
lessonContent:
Reciprocity can sustain cooperation.
Simple rules often outperform complex ones.
Forgiveness prevents endless feuds.
Respond to behaviour, not intentions.
Share this: apply one equal-and-opposite response in a repeating situation.

title: Poor But Locked In
question: A Nash equilibrium can be inefficient and still remain stable.
correctExplanation: True. No one can improve alone, which is enough to hold a wasteful arrangement in place.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Stability and efficiency are independent properties, so a poor but locked-in outcome is perfectly possible.
lessonContent:
Independent standards can disagree.
Locked-in outcomes may be poor.
Collective improvement needs coordination.
Look for ways to change the whole game.
Share this: identify one stable situation everyone wishes were different.

title: No Regret
question: At a Nash equilibrium, each player regrets their choice given what the others did.
correctExplanation: False. By definition no player could have done better by switching alone, so there is no regret in that sense.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. A player might wish the whole outcome were different, but given the others' choices their own move was best.
lessonContent:
No single change improves your position.
Regret concerns joint alternatives, not solo ones.
Distinguish your choice from the outcome.
Check each move against the others'.
Share this: ask whether you would change your move given the others'.

title: Free Rider
question: Free riding is an example of a collective action problem.
correctExplanation: True. Benefiting without contributing undermines the group effort that produces the benefit.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. When contributions are voluntary and benefits shared, each individual gains by letting others pay the cost.
lessonContent:
Shared benefits invite non-contribution.
Voluntary efforts are vulnerable to free riding.
Excludability changes incentives.
Design rules that reward contribution.
Share this: notice one shared effort you benefit from without joining.

title: Arms Race
question: An arms race can be modelled as a prisoner's dilemma.
correctExplanation: True. Each side arms to avoid falling behind, and both end up worse off than if neither had.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Mutual restraint would be better, but each side fears the other's advantage, producing the same dilemma structure.
lessonContent:
Competition can trap both parties.
Fear of falling behind drives escalation.
Mutual restraint needs enforcement.
Look for ways to change the stakes.
Share this: find one escalation that both sides would prefer to stop.
